en.title: Before cities and markets: the political economy of survival in the Paleolithic
en.deck: Comparative archaeological investigation of production, energy, cooperation, food risk, material exchange, social organization and power before farming, from earliest lithic technologies to Late Pleistocene foragers.
en.regime: Diverse Pleistocene foraging systems organize production, risk management, material access and social cooperation without presupposing states or monetary markets.
en.key_risk: Treating first archaeological appearances as dates of universal invention, or projecting modern states, prices, gender roles and class structures onto fragmentary evidence.

pt-BR.title: Antes das cidades e dos mercados: a economia política da sobrevivência no Paleolítico
pt-BR.deck: Investigação arqueológica comparativa da produção, energia, cooperação, risco alimentar, circulação de materiais, organização social e poder antes da agricultura, das primeiras ferramentas ao Pleistoceno tardio.
pt-BR.regime: Sistemas coletores diversos durante o Pleistoceno organizam produção, risco, acesso a materiais e cooperação sem pressupor Estados ou mercados monetários.
pt-BR.key_risk: Tratar primeiras evidências arqueológicas como datas de invenção universal ou projetar Estados, preços, papéis sexuais e classes modernos em vestígios fragmentários.

contrary_evidence: The same lithic material can arise from mobility, direct procurement or exchange; no unique monetary or legal regime follows from geochemical sourcing.
Grave gifts and conspicuous burials are not equivalent to a community-wide distribution of land title, income or durable elite power.
Ethnographic behavior of modern foragers generates hypotheses and is not direct observation of Pleistocene societies.
Environmental variability is a plausible contributor to technological change but cannot alone demonstrate why specific innovations spread.
The fire-making claim at Barnham is distinct from older and differently assessed claims about controlled fire use.
limitations: Archaeological visibility is uneven and biased toward durable materials, excavated sites and particular burial practices.
Dates are approximate site-specific archaeological first appearances, not universal human milestones.
The chart compares only documented antiquities using millions of years before present; it is not a measure of technological sophistication or evolutionary progress.
Ancient DNA and present-day ethnography cover selected groups and should not be generalized to the entire Paleolithic.
Numerical GDP, income inequality, population and wage series are deliberately absent for prehistoric periods due to lack of comparable observations.

producer_checks.information_cutoff: 2 November 2026; source literature spanning 2011–2026 and source-specific dating conventions; no fast-moving contemporary incident claims.
producer_checks.editorial_novelty: First case in the historical civilizations editorial line; research starts before agricultural settlement, examines economic production, material circulation, political limits and social differentiation with testable alternatives.
producer_checks.visual_signature: Two bilingual-parallel evidence tables, two numeric chronological bar charts with identical series [3.3,2.9,1.76,0.32] million years and [400,125,65,34] thousand years BP, two causal chains and one seven-context regional map.
producer_checks.source_check: 18 matching scholarly/institutional reference URLs per locale, including independent archaeological analysis of Sunghir grave contexts and original Nature fire-making article.
producer_checks.bilingual_parity: 16 equivalent analytical heading sections including source notes, 18 identical scholarly source URLs, aligned two chronological bar charts, one flow and one geographical map per language.
producer_checks.research_depth: English ~4,130 substantive words / 32,991 chars; PT-BR ~4,423 substantive words / 35,481 chars; both substantially exceed 8,000 substantive characters.
producer_checks.methodology: Source triangulation via stratigraphy, lithic studies, isotope sourcing, palaeoecology, ancient DNA, comparative ethnography and explicit nonidentification of modern economic institutions where evidence cannot show them.
